name: Isfahan and New Julfa: silk, city and forced movement
geographicPrecision: City locator; New Julfa lies south of the river. Carpet workshops were also in Yazd and Kashan; an individual carpet is not securely assigned to this point.

interval.label: Selected Safavid capital phase, 1597–98 to 1722
interval.note: Start follows the conventional 1597–98 capital transfer, plotted at 1598. The endpoint marks the selected capital phase, not Isfahan’s existence or every later Safavid dynastic claim.

question: Who made a prosperous capital—and whose movement was coerced?
summary: Isfahan’s prosperity joined urban building, rural silk, skilled making, commerce and household work. New Julfa’s institutions developed after forced relocation. The carpet, merchant correspondence and a later family letter make different relationships visible without identifying one common experience, a particular weaver or a route for this object.

sections.title: A new centre within an older city
sections.text: Isfahan did not begin with the conventional capital transfer of 1597–98. Haneda and Matthee describe gradual development and a mobile royal household. A new governmental and commercial centre grew southwest of the older one. Shops, caravansaries, bathhouses and coffeehouses gathered around the royal square and adjacent bazaar; the older centre remained important. A bazaar entrance stood at the square’s north end. This relationship makes the square one connection within a larger city, rather than a picture of its entire economy. These named relationships explain how buying, lodging and service work shared urban space. New Julfa lay south of the Zayandarud, rather than inside every picture of the royal square.

citations.locator: Isfahan as the Safavid Capital: new commercial centre and urban quarters

sections.title: Silk connected several kinds of making
sections.text: Munroe distinguishes rural raw-silk producers, private urban workshops and court production. Dyers, weavers, embroiderers and designers contributed different skills. Repeated patterns required coordination between design and material work. The Met identifies the selected Doria carpet as silk pile with metal-wrapped thread, made with knotting and brocading. This is a particular carpet technique, not every cloth process in the essay. The type is associated with several Iranian centres, including Isfahan, Yazd and Kashan; its appearance cannot name the individual workshop or weavers.

sections.title: A prosperous quarter followed forced movement
sections.text: In 1604, state-directed destruction and deportation uprooted Armenians from Old Julfa. Settlement at New Julfa began in 1605. Ghougassian distinguishes mercantile deportees from other displaced people and identifies later movements of artisans. Houses, churches, craft and service work helped make the new community. Painters and metalworkers appear beside gardeners, porters and other laborers in the account. Privileges for some merchants and later commercial achievement do not turn coercion into voluntary migration or establish equal wealth and freedom within the quarter.

citations.locator: Origin, settlement, and population; Society and administration

sections.title: Commerce required relationships and information
sections.text: Tajiryan’s study describes the Girach-Mirman brothers pooling funds in New Julfa in 1656. Their particular gem-trading business paired capital with travelling agents and correspondence. A translated 1700 letter about turquoise exposes disagreement over prices and the difficulty of obtaining goods. Negotiating and sharing information were work, alongside transporting or making things. This example does not document a silk transaction or the selected carpet’s journey. Reading it beside the urban and craft accounts adds practical coordination without reducing the city to a ruler’s building program.

deeperReading.title: A household could contain unequal dependencies
deeperReading.text: Ghougassian’s synthesis draws on fragmentary histories, colophons, letters and community records. Its particular seventeenth-century wills reveal houses, commercial holdings, servants and enslaved dependants; some grants of freedom were delayed until the owner’s death. These examples make dependence part of a prosperous community’s history. They do not supply an average household, establish that every servant was enslaved or make all residents wealthy merchants. The original wills were not independently consulted here. An account of collective institutions therefore needs questions about who controlled property and whose work sustained it.

deeperReading.title: A later family voice changes the question
deeperReading.text: The UCLA account presents Anna Khatoon’s letter from New Julfa to her husband, a textile merchant. Its supplied translation includes family greetings, a request for his safe return and an enclosed lock of hair. The rendered date, 9 August 1747, is later than the entire 1598–1722 case. This comparison brings separation and family communication into view without becoming testimony to the 1604 deportation. It is one mediated voice, not every woman’s experience. Together with commercial correspondence, it suggests that letters could carry different concerns within distant trade relationships. The original manuscript and Armenian translation were not independently checked, and the author’s hypotheses about literacy or the hair’s purpose remain hypotheses.

evidenceReading.title: A carpet, a business disagreement and a later family message
evidenceReading.introduction: These are editorial paraphrases of different records. The supplied image supports observation; catalogue and translated documents supply other claims. Their dates and limits remain separate.

items.label: An attractive surface is not a workshop address
items.text: The photograph shows repeated curving forms, a central field and borders. The catalogue identifies silk pile, metal-wrapped thread and an Iranian type once wrongly called Polonaise.
items.interpretation: Visible arrangement can be checked in the image. Material, attribution and collecting history require the catalogue. Several centres are named for the type; this does not establish an Isfahan address, Armenian maker, named buyer or exact export route for accession 50.190.5.

citations.locator: Actual supplied photograph; opening description and Artwork Details

items.label: A translated disagreement reveals coordination
items.text: Tajiryan presents a 1700 exchange between Herapet di Martin and Amirbēk di Vardan concerning turquoise prices and obtaining supplies.
items.interpretation: The particular exchange makes negotiation and information visible. It is a gem-trading example, not a carpet shipment or an account of every Julfan firm. The selected paper and translation were consulted; the original Armenian archive was not independently collated.

items.label: A later letter offers a particular household perspective
items.text: The UCLA account supplies translated passages from Anna Khatoon’s family letter, including greetings, a request for her husband’s safe return and the date rendered as 9 August 1747.
items.interpretation: Its later date matters: this is outside the atlas case, not eyewitness evidence for 1604. One letter cannot stand for every woman, household or displaced person. No independent translation, calendar conversion or explanation of the enclosed hair’s purpose was established here.

familyActivity.title: What can a carpet show—and what needs another record?
steps: Look at the supplied carpet image. Point to a repeated curving form and a border. Describe their arrangement without guessing the maker’s identity.
Read the source capsule together. Make three cards: visible observation, catalogue identification and a dated written account.
Place “the border repeats a form,” “the carpet uses silk pile” and “New Julfa settlement followed forced movement” with the records that support them.
Write one supported statement about work or movement and one question about a household or maker that these records cannot answer.
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: the Met identifies this as a seventeenth-century Iranian carpet type, made with silk pile and metal-wrapped thread, without securely assigning it to one workshop. Ghougassian dates forced movement from Old Julfa to 1604 and the start of New Julfa settlement to 1605. A particular merchant firm’s records show commercial coordination; a family letter dated 1747 is a later comparison outside the case. The carpet image cannot establish those events or identify all the people who made it.

review.reviewer: Codex selected source consultation and internal author QA; not independent historian or Armenian community approval
review.scope: Urban relationships, making, forced settlement and particular commercial/household records. Four selected rereads retain earlier dated scopes; two new textual sources distinguish scholarship and a supplied translation. Three further source records support two modern published property references and a verbal bridge connection. Original case, claims, comparison texts, object order and image bytes remain intact.
limitations: The 1598–1722 case, 1601–1700 carpet envelope, selected 1604–1747 record frame and modern publications are separate. The 1747 letter is later comparison, not 1604 testimony.
No original chronicle, will, archival inventory or Armenian letter independently collated. Selected translations and institutional scholarship do not represent all residents, workers or women.

The Met essay’s compressed 1598 relocation sentence is excluded; the separately sourced 1604/1605 sequence is retained. No settled deportee total, individual carpet workshop, buyer or itinerary inferred.

Two modern published property-reference points are adopted, with a textual bridge relationship. No measured street or river plan, bridge coordinate, quarter boundary, household or workshop location, route, copied figure or new image is adopted. Local Iranica captures returned 403; exposed article text was consulted without bypass.
Independent historical/community review, real family use, human screen-reader/device behavior and physical print acceptance remain open.
